interpretation: Stop before acceptance and reconsider the audit-disclosure boundary.

claims.claim: It is the standard or common position in device transactions that the buyer owns the hardware while the software remains subject to licence terms accepted at setup.
claims.evidence: The usual answer is that you bought the hardware, while the software remains subject to terms you accepted somewhere between the unboxing and the first tap.
claims.verification_question: Is it a standard or widely documented industry/legal position that device buyers own the hardware while software remains under a licence accepted during setup, such that this can fairly be called 'the usual answer'?

claims.claim: A landlord has the legal right to evict a tenant under terms the tenant agreed to.
claims.evidence: A landlord can evict you under rules you agreed to
claims.verification_question: Is it accurate as a general legal matter that landlords may evict tenants under contractually agreed terms, across the relevant jurisdiction(s) this essay addresses?

claims.claim: A seller of physical goods does not ordinarily have the legal right to re-enter a buyer's home and remove purchased items.
claims.evidence: a seller doesn't ordinarily get to walk into your house and remove the kitchen because the appliance company changed its mind
claims.verification_question: Is it accurate as a general legal/commercial matter that sellers of physical goods have no ordinary right to reclaim items after a completed sale by entering the buyer's property?

claims.claim: Remote or post-sale disabling of device features is widely treated as normal or ordinary practice by consumers and/or the industry.
claims.evidence: the digital version of that arrangement is treated as ordinary
claims.verification_question: Is there evidence that post-sale remote disabling of device features is broadly accepted or treated as ordinary by consumers, industry, or regulators rather than being contested?

claims.claim: Device software licence agreements are typically too long for a consumer to reasonably read.
claims.evidence: the contract is longer than anyone can reasonably read
claims.verification_question: Is there documented evidence (e.g., studies on EULA length or reading time) that device software licence agreements are generally too lengthy for a consumer to read in a reasonable time?

claims.claim: Many users who encounter a default setting will not change it.
claims.verification_question: Is there empirical evidence (e.g., studies on default persistence) showing that a substantial majority or large share of users leave defaults unchanged?

claims.claim: Users fail to change defaults primarily because doing so requires attention, time, and confidence that the alternative will work as well.
claims.evidence: changing it takes attention, time, and confidence that the alternative will work as well
claims.verification_question: What research or evidence identifies attention cost, time cost, and performance uncertainty as the principal reasons users do not change defaults?

claims.claim: Most users leave a preselected software setting unchanged rather than switching to an alternative.
claims.evidence: most people will leave the setting alone
claims.verification_question: Is there empirical evidence (e.g., behavioral-economics research or platform usage data) showing that most users do not change preselected software defaults when given a choice screen?
